That's a part of it, but I think there's a more central issue.

If you tear every genuinely destructive crime or sin down to its roots, you find the exact same dynamic - one person negating the will of another person. That is, in fact, exactly what distinguishes crimes and sins from non-crimes and non-sins - the fact that the "victim" has had his will negated. Rape is sex against the victim's will. Theft is the transfer of property against the victim's will. Murder is the taking of life against the victim's will. And so on - in every case, the significant fact - the thing that defines the act as a crime or sin - is the fact that it's carried out against the will of the victim.

So the "bad person" is the person who has no concern for the wills of others. That can spring from a sense of superiority, and there's often at least some measure of that, but that's not the only basis for it. Many don't go so far as to really consider themselves "superior," since they don't really recognize other people as actual people at all, inferior, superior or otherwise. They don't even consider the fact that other people have internal lives - values and beliefs and desires and norms - that are just as real and just as meaningful as their own. To them, their own lives and their own desires are all that matter, and other people are just sort of self-propelled props - just part of the backdrop to the all-important spectacle of their own lives.

I would like to counter 1 point. Upward mobility is a flat out lie. The resources are not infinite for any kind of economic plan. Those that control those resources do not give them up easily and will do something to take over anything "new" that bites into their control.

But upward mobility on the personal/family level has more to do with how you use your resources (which you can get through earnings working for a company) than it does garnering sections of market share (which businesses will absolutely fight tooth and nail to protect). I think there's an important distinction there.

Now if you run a small business (or medium or large), then you're naturally in a different group than most people, and what impacts you is quite different.

But I think this confuses personal upward mobility (generally financed from working for some company) which is based on how you spend your earnings, with for instance starting up a new businesses and trying to capture market share from other businesses( which they will jealously guard). The business world wants to get at your earnings, but they don't intentionally lock you out from earning more than enough money to start working on financial independence to some degree (which you could use to finance a lifestyle higher than what your job earnings could provide if you chose to).

If you have trouble with upward mobility in the US, then the first place you need to look at is yourself and how you choose to spend what you earn. You may need to earn more, but the vast majority of the time that's not the problem.

Most people have a spending problem (either current or service on debt), not an earning problem. Some people of course don't like to see it that way, because some it's comforting to blame something external for the opportunities that exist, but which they have chosen not to participate in because they wanted to do something else instead.

There are numerous paths to this, but the one I'm thinking of is just plain old investing (i.e.g. index shares in dow, spidr, etc., super easy to get into and arguably the best investment you can make at moderate risk levels), an investment account will run anywhere from $500-$2500 to open, and earn you between generally 5% and 12% annually depending on how things go. Any adult willing to be honest with themselves, over 28, has blown way more than that on trivial things like Subway, coffee, whatever.

That's not bad, but it is real. And it really means that instead of setting yourself up to have your money make you more money without you working for it (which it takes a very long time and a lot of capital to reach quit your job income, it starts as a trickle) you as an individual have chosen to do other things. Again, not good or bad, but it's not the fault of society or the system if there's a path to increase your financial independence or standing and have chosen not to follow it. That's on the individual.
